standard.title: Sentence boundary punctuation
standard.description: understand that written language uses punctuation such as full stops, question marks and exclamation marks, and uses capital letters for familiar proper nouns
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can identify punctuation as a feature of written text different from letters, and recognise capital letters at sentence beginnings (AC9EFLA09). They have not yet understood the specific signalling functions of sentence-ending punctuation marks or the use of capital letters for proper nouns.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students understand sentence boundary punctuation — full stops, question marks, exclamation marks — and use capital letters for familiar proper nouns.

nodes.label: Punctuation marks signal sentence endings
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify full stops, question marks and exclamation marks as sentence-ending punctuation and explain that each signals a different type of sentence.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify all three sentence-ending punctuation marks by name and match each to its sentence type (statement, question, exclamation).
nodes.typical_width: Identify full stops, question marks and exclamation marks in written texts, name each correctly, explain which sentence type each signals, and respond to them when reading aloud (pausing, intonation change).
wider: Explore how the same words with different end punctuation create different sentences — e.g. 'You did it.' vs 'You did it?' vs 'You did it!'
Examine how writers use exclamation marks for effect and discuss whether overuse reduces their impact
success_criteria: Student identifies and names all three sentence-ending punctuation marks correctly
Student matches each punctuation mark to its sentence type

nodes.label: Punctuation guides reading aloud
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use intonation and pauses in response to sentence-ending punctuation when reading.
nodes.minimum_width: Read a short passage aloud, pausing at full stops and adjusting intonation at question marks and exclamation marks.
nodes.typical_width: Consistently use appropriate intonation and pausing in response to sentence boundary punctuation when reading aloud — full stops signal pause and drop, question marks signal rising intonation, exclamation marks signal emphasis.
wider: Listen to recordings of the same text read with and without attention to punctuation, and discuss the difference in meaning and expression
Practise reading dialogue that includes multiple punctuation types, attending to how each mark shapes the character's voice

response_modes.reason: Translating punctuation knowledge into consistent oral reading requires repeated rehearsal. Students may know the rule but not yet apply it automatically — oral reading practice across varied texts builds the habit.

success_criteria: Student pauses at full stops and end-of-sentence marks when reading aloud
Student adjusts intonation at question marks (rising) and exclamation marks (emphasis)

nodes.label: Capital letters for proper nouns
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify familiar proper nouns and explain that they require capital letters.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two familiar proper nouns in a text and explain why they use capital letters.
nodes.typical_width: Identify proper nouns — names of people, places, days, months, holidays — in texts and writing, apply capital letters to familiar proper nouns, and explain that proper nouns are specific names that always take capitals.
wider: Distinguish between common nouns and proper nouns in context (e.g. 'city' vs 'Sydney'), and write sentences using both
Explore why days and months are capitalised — link to the concept of proper names
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who limit capitalisation to personal names will systematically miscapitalise place names, days and months in writing — this pattern, once established, persists into N4's application task and beyond into independent writing.

response_modes.reason: Students typically know names of people take capitals but often miss place names, days of the week, months and holidays. Encountering a range of proper noun categories resolves the misconception that only personal names require capitalisation.

success_criteria: Student correctly identifies at least two proper nouns in a text and explains why each is capitalised
Student writes familiar proper nouns with correct capitalisation in their own writing

nodes.label: Writing with sentence punctuation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can apply sentence boundary punctuation and proper noun capitalisation in their own writing.
nodes.minimum_width: Write at least two different sentence types (statement and question) using correct end punctuation, and capitalise at least one proper noun.
nodes.typical_width: Write statements, questions and exclamations using correct end punctuation, capitalise proper nouns and sentence-opening capitals, and identify and correct punctuation errors in given sentences.
wider: Write a short dialogue using multiple sentence types with correct punctuation throughout
Edit a deliberately un-punctuated passage, adding sentence boundary punctuation and proper noun capitalisation

response_modes.reason: Applying punctuation consistently in writing requires sustained practice beyond recognition tasks. Writing and editing tasks build the automatic application that transfers into independent writing.

success_criteria: Student correctly punctuates at least two different sentence types in their own writing
Student capitalises proper nouns correctly in at least two examples in their writing
